facts.statement: Terminonaris is an extinct genus of pholidosaurid crocodyliforms belonging to the subgroup Mesoeucrocodylia.
facts.quote: Terminonaris is a genus of extinct pholidosaurid crocodyliforms that lived during the Late Cretaceous (Cenomanian and Turonian) epoch.

facts.statement: Henry Fairfield Osborn described the genus in 1904, initially naming it Teleorhinus before suggesting Terminonaris as an alternative name.
facts.quote: When Henry Fairfield Osborn described this taxon in 1904, he named it Teleorhinus, but also suggested alternative name Terminonaris in the same publication, considering the case that the former was preoccpuied.

facts.statement: The skull of the largest known individual of Terminonaris is 109.6 cm long.
facts.quote: The skull of the largest individual is 109.6 cm long.

facts.statement: Its elongated snout and thin interlocking teeth suggest Terminonaris hunted fish, small mammals, and possibly small dinosaurs.
facts.quote: The elongated snout and the long, relatively thin interlocking teeth suggest that Terminonaris was a hunter of fish, small mammals and possibly small dinosaurs.

facts.statement: Terminonaris is the most derived crocodile-relative known to possess scleral rings.
facts.quote: It is also the most derived crocodile-relative found to possess scleral rings

facts.statement: Terminonaris inhabited the Western Interior Seaway, an inland sea stretching from the Gulf of Mexico to the Arctic Ocean during the Late Cretaceous.
facts.quote: Terminonaris inhabited the Western Interior Seaway, an inland sea that stretched from the Gulf of Mexico to the Arctic Ocean during Late Cretaceous time.

facts.statement: Terminonaris likely stayed near the shore and only ventured into the warm, salty seaway water to hunt for fish.
facts.quote: The creature probably kept close to the shore, venturing into the seaway's warm salty water only to hunt for fish.

facts.statement: Seven fossil specimens of Terminonaris have been found, six in North America and one in Europe.
facts.quote: Seven fossil specimens of Terminonaris have been discovered and all are from the Northern Hemisphere: six from North America and one from Europe.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Terminonaris originated in Europe or Texas, with recent evidence suggesting a Texas origin and northward dispersal.
facts.quote: Scientists originally thought that Terminonaris originated in Europe, and then migrated across the Atlantic Ocean and dispersed throughout North America. However, it now seems more likely that Terminonaris originated in Texas and then dispersed northward.

facts.statement: The oldest known Terminonaris fossil, found in Texas, lived about 96 million years ago.
facts.quote: The oldest, from Texas, lived about 96 million years ago.

facts.statement: The bones of Big Bert were discovered in 1991 in the Favel Formation near the Carrot River in Saskatchewan.
facts.quote: His bones were discovered in 1991 in an outcrop of the Favel Formation along the banks of the Carrot River in the Pasquia Hills of Saskatchewan.

facts.statement: Big Bert was discovered by paleontologist Tim Tokaryk with the help of local fossil hunter Dickson Hardie.
facts.quote: The discovery was made by paleontologist Tim Tokaryk from the Royal Saskatchewan Museum, guided by local fossil hunter Dickson Hardie.

facts.statement: Big Bert lived about 92 million years ago near the eastern shoreline of the Western Interior Seaway.
facts.quote: Big Bert is believed to have lived about 92 million years ago, at a time when the Carrot River area was near the eastern shoreline of the Western Interior Seaway.

facts.statement: Brian Condon discovered a 96 million-year-old Terminonaris fossil in 2005 near Lake Lewisville in Texas.
facts.quote: In 2005 an amateur fossil enthusiast and rural mail carrier named Brian Condon discovered a 96 million year old Terminonaris while fossil-hunting close to his home on Lake Lewisville near Dallas, Texas.

facts.statement: The Texas fossils discovered by Brian Condon are the oldest and southernmost known examples of Terminonaris.
facts.quote: They turned out to be the oldest examples of Terminonaris, as well as the southernmost found to date.

facts.statement: Terminonaris lived between 100.5 and 89.8 million years ago during the Cenomanian to Turonian stages.
facts.quote: Time range: Cenomanian to Turonian (100.5 to 89.8 million years ago)
